claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets are governed primarily by variations in grain-boundary segregation.
Grain-boundary segregation leads to nanoclustering of Cr, Mn, and Ni.
Nanoclustering of Cr, Mn, and Ni modifies grain-boundary cohesion.
Reducing the number of constituent elements alters segregation behavior and mitigates intermediate-temperature embrittlement.
Single-phase FCC HEAs and MEAs containing three or more elements from Al, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni can exhibit rapid ductility loss between approximately 400°C and 800°C.
In equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20, Cr, Mn, and Ni rapidly segregate separately to grain boundaries during intermediate-temperature deformation.
Cr, Mn, and Ni nanoclusters at grain boundaries reduce local grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion promotes grain-boundary crack initiation and premature failure.
Removing one or more elements in quaternary or ternary subsets may change segregation dynamics and reduce grain-boundary embrittlement.
Relative to the quinary alloy, quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit reduced or altered clustering of Cr, Mn, or Ni at grain boundaries.
Reduced or altered grain-boundary clustering in the lower-component alloys will produce less ductility loss.
Quaternary and ternary alloys will have improved overall mechanical performance during intermediate-temperature deformation relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline undergoes temperature-associated strength and elongation decreases and grain-boundary cracking during intermediate-temperature tensile deformation.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply only to similarly processed, single-phase FCC HEAs or MEAs under intermediate-temperature deformation.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to multiphase alloys or alloys with significant precipitate formation.
Preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases can redirect rapidly segregating Cr, Mn, and Ni away from grain boundaries and thereby avoid ductility loss.
The quantitative relationship between constituent count, segregation extent, and mechanical-property changes is not established.
